topics.title: Climate, weather and ripening
topics.summary: Heat, sunlight and water decide how ripe grapes get. Climate is the long-term pattern of a place; weather is what happens in a given year and explains vintage variation.

sections.heading: What the vine needs
points: Sunlight, heat, water, carbon dioxide and nutrients. Photosynthesis turns CO₂ and water into sugar using sunlight.
Growth starts at about 10 °C; photosynthesis works best between roughly 18 and 33 °C. Above that the vine shuts down to save water.
Too much vigour (water, nitrogen) means leaves and shoots grow at the expense of the fruit; a little stress focuses the vine on ripening.

causes.result: energy goes into the grapes: smaller berries, more concentration

sections.heading: The growing cycle
points: Winter dormancy (Nov–Mar in the north): the vine rests; pruning is done now.
Budburst (Mar–Apr): sensitive to spring frost.
Flowering and fruit set (May–Jun): needs warm, dry, calm weather. Poor fruit set gives coulure (flowers fail to set) or millerandage (uneven, small seedless berries).
Veraison (Jul–Aug): berries soften and change colour; sugar starts to build.
Ripening and harvest (Sep–Oct): sugar rises, acidity falls, colour, tannin and aromas mature. In the Southern Hemisphere everything is six months later.

causes.factor: Cold or wet weather at flowering

causes.effect: sugar up, acidity down, tannin and flavour mature
causes.result: harvest date sets the balance of the wine

sections.heading: Climate types
points: Classified by the average temperature of the growing season: cool up to 16.5 °C, moderate 16.5–18.5 °C, warm 18.5–21 °C, hot above 21 °C.
Continental: big difference between summer and winter, short summers, cold winters, spring frost risk (Burgundy, Champagne).
Maritime: small difference between seasons thanks to the sea; mild, often rainy (Bordeaux).
Mediterranean: warm, dry summers and mild, wet winters (southern France, much of the New World).
Cool climates: lighter body, higher acidity, green and citrus fruit. Hot climates: riper fruit, more alcohol and body, softer acidity.

causes.result: lighter body, high acid, green and red fruit
full body, high alcohol, ripe black or tropical fruit

sections.heading: What changes temperature
points: Latitude: most vineyards lie between 30° and 50°; nearer the poles grapes struggle to ripen.
Altitude: about 0.6 °C cooler per 100 m; high vineyards keep acidity in hot countries (Mendoza, Salta).
Slope and aspect: slopes facing the equator catch more sun; cold air drains down slopes, reducing frost.
Water bodies: seas, lakes and rivers moderate temperatures and reflect light (Mosel, Finger Lakes).
Ocean currents and fog: cold currents (Humboldt, Benguela, California) cool coastal areas; fog slows ripening.
Soil: stones and dark soils store heat; wet clay soils stay cool.
Diurnal range: cool nights keep acidity and aromas while warm days ripen sugar.

causes.factor: Cold ocean current and coastal fog
causes.effect: cooler, slower ripening near the coast
sugar builds by day, acid and aromas kept by night

sections.heading: Sunlight and water
points: More sunlight means more photosynthesis; slopes facing the equator, long summer days at high latitude and clear skies all help.
The vine needs about 500–700 mm of water a year depending on heat, ideally in winter and spring.
Too much water: vigour, dilution, rot. Too little: stress, stopped ripening, damaged vines.
Where rain is low, irrigation (drip, sprinkler, flood) is used, often under controlled deficit to limit vigour.

sections.heading: Weather hazards
points: Spring frost kills new shoots; prevented by wind machines, heaters, sprinklers (ice protects the buds) or late pruning.
Winter freeze below about −20 °C can kill vines (Washington, Canada, New York).
Hail tears leaves and berries; nets are used in Argentina.
Rain at harvest swells berries and spreads rot.
Drought and heat stress stop ripening; fire can taint grapes with smoke.
Climate change: earlier harvests, higher alcohol, new regions (England) becoming viable.

topics.title: Growing the grapes
topics.summary: The grower decides the site, plant material, training, canopy, yield and harvest. Each choice trades quality against cost and quantity.

sections.heading: Site and soil
points: A good site has the right temperature for the variety, enough sun and access to water without waterlogging.
Soil matters mostly for water and heat: free-draining gravel and stone warm up and drain after rain; clay holds water and stays cool.
Fertile soils give vigorous vines; poorer soils limit vigour and yields.

causes.result: late varieties ripen (Cabernet on Médoc gravel)

sections.heading: Plant material
points: Almost all wine comes from Vitis vinifera. Varieties can mutate (Pinot Noir → Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc); growers choose clones for yield, disease resistance or flavour.
Crossings are new varieties from two vinifera parents (Pinotage, Müller-Thurgau). Hybrids cross vinifera with other species for cold or disease resistance.
Phylloxera, an aphid, eats vinifera roots. The fix is grafting onto American rootstocks, chosen for soil, vigour and drought tolerance.
Places phylloxera never reached or cannot survive: Chile, parts of South Australia, sandy or volcanic soils (Santorini).

sections.heading: Training and pruning
points: Winter pruning sets how many buds (and so shoots and bunches) the vine carries.
Spur pruning keeps short stubs on a permanent cordon; cane pruning lays down one or two long canes each year (Guyot).
Bush vines (head-trained, no wires) suit hot, dry, windy places: the canopy shades the fruit (Châteauneuf, Barossa, Priorat).
Vertical shoot positioning (VSP) gives a neat wall of leaves for sun exposure and machine work.
High training keeps fruit away from frost or ground humidity; pergolas give airflow in humid places (Rías Baixas, Vinho Verde).

sections.heading: Canopy and yield
points: Canopy management balances leaves and fruit: shoot thinning, leaf removal around the bunches, hedging.
Leaf removal increases sun and airflow on grapes: better ripening, less rot, but sunburn risk in hot places.
Yield is set by vine density, pruning and green harvesting (cutting bunches before veraison).
Very high yields usually dilute flavour; very low yields cost more but are not automatically better.

causes.factor: Leaf removal around the fruit zone
causes.effect: more sunlight and air on the bunches
the vine’s energy spread over more fruit

sections.heading: Pests, diseases and approaches
points: Fungal: powdery mildew (oidium) and downy mildew (peronospora) attack leaves and fruit; grey rot (Botrytis) spoils bunches in damp weather; trunk diseases kill old vines.
Controlled by sprays (copper and sulfur allowed in organics), canopy airflow and resistant varieties.
Viruses spread by insects or nematodes; birds and animals eat fruit.
Integrated pest management: monitor and treat only when needed. Organic: no synthetic chemicals. Biodynamic: organic plus preparations and a calendar.

causes.result: more spraying and careful canopy work

sections.heading: Harvest
points: Timing balances sugar, acidity, tannin ripeness and flavour against weather risk; picking early keeps acidity, later gives riper fruit and more alcohol.
Hand picking allows whole bunches, sorting and steep slopes, but is slow and costly.
Machine picking is fast and cheap, works at night when it is cool, but needs flat land and breaks berries.

causes.factor: Night machine harvesting in hot regions

causes.result: needed for whole-bunch, sparkling and botrytised wines

topics.title: Winemaking basics
topics.summary: The tools every winemaker uses: yeast, temperature, oxygen, SO₂, vessels and oak, lees, MLC, blending, clarification and closures.

sections.heading: Fermentation and yeast
points: Yeast turn sugar into alcohol, CO₂ and heat, plus aroma compounds.
Ambient (wild) yeast can add complexity but are less predictable; cultured yeast are reliable and chosen for style.
Fermentation stops when sugar runs out, alcohol gets too high (about 15–16%), temperature is too high or low, or the winemaker stops it.

sections.heading: Oxygen and sulfur dioxide
points: Protective winemaking keeps oxygen out (inert gas, cool temperatures, SO₂) to keep fresh primary fruit.
Controlled oxygen softens tannins and adds complexity (barrels, racking, micro-oxygenation).
SO₂ is an antioxidant and antiseptic: it protects against oxidation and microbes. Too much smells of struck matches.

sections.heading: Vessels and oak
points: Inert vessels (stainless steel, concrete lined) add nothing; easy to clean and control temperature.
Oak adds flavour (vanilla, toast, spice) and lets in a little oxygen, which softens tannin and adds complexity.
Effect depends on size (small barriques 225 L give more), age (new gives most), toast level, and origin (French: subtle spice and toast; American: vanilla and coconut).
Oak staves or chips in tank are a cheap, quick way to add oak flavour without the oxygen effect.

sections.heading: Lees, MLC and blending
points: Lees are dead yeast; long contact adds texture and bready or creamy flavours; stirring (bâtonnage) strengthens the effect.
Malolactic conversion: bacteria turn sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid, adding buttery notes. Standard for reds, a choice for whites.
Blending improves balance, complexity and consistency: varieties, sites, vintages, vessels.

sections.heading: Clarification, stabilisation and bottling
points: Clarification: settling and racking, fining (bentonite, egg white, gelatine, pea protein) to remove haze or harsh tannin, then filtration.
Depth filtration removes larger particles; surface (membrane) filtration can remove yeast and bacteria (sterile filtration).
Tartrate stabilisation (chilling) stops harmless crystals forming in bottle; protein stabilisation (bentonite) stops haze in whites.
Closures: natural cork lets in a little oxygen but can carry TCA (cork taint); screwcaps keep fruit fresh and avoid taint; synthetic corks are cheap but less airtight.

causes.result: needed for wines with residual sugar or no MLC

topics.title: White winemaking
topics.summary: Fewer steps than red winemaking. Almost every decision trades protecting fresh primary fruit against building texture and complexity.

sections.heading: Skin contact
points: Usual path: crush, run off the free-run juice, press the rest quickly. Little skin contact means little oxidation.
Whole-bunch pressing (uncrushed grapes into the press) is the gentlest option: least oxidation, purer and more delicate wines.
Some aromatic varieties get a few hours of cold skin contact (too cold to ferment) for more flavour and texture.
Orange or amber wines ferment white grapes on their skins like a red. Traditional in Georgia, Slovenia and Friuli-Venezia Giulia.
Orange wine taste: noticeable tannin, dried fruit, dried herbs, hay, nuts.

causes.result: orange wine with grip and dried-fruit notes

sections.heading: Clarity of the juice
points: Fresh juice carries skin and pulp fragments (solids). Fermenting them can give off-flavours or a stuck fermentation, so juice is clarified first.
Methods: settling, centrifuge, fining, filtration. Settling is gentle but slow; centrifuge or filter when tank space and time matter.
Leaving some solids can add complexity and richer texture (and may help resist oxidation), but risks off-flavours, so it is rare for pure varietal styles.

sections.heading: Fermentation temperature and vessel
points: Whites ferment at about 12–22 °C.
Too cold: pear-drop aromas and varietal fruit not captured. Warmer: more complex non-fruit aromas, but varietal fruit can be lost.
Stainless steel tanks allow precise temperature control.
Barrels are harder to control but small and usually in cool cellars, so they lose heat well; barrel ferments still run at the warm end of the range.

causes.result: rounder texture, toasty notes, more complexity

sections.heading: After fermentation
points: Oak: mature in barrel, or keep in an inert vessel, with or without oak staves or chips.
Fine lees: add texture and flavour. Lees stirring (mixing the settled lees back into the wine) strengthens the effect.
Malolactic conversion: allow it for a rounder, creamier, buttery wine with softer acidity and less primary fruit; block it (chill and add SO₂) to keep acidity and fruit.
Blending: for fruity styles mainly about consistency; for Chardonnay, batches with different lees, MLC and oak are blended for complexity.
Clarification and stabilisation: pale wines show any haze, so most are fined and/or filtered. Wines with residual sugar are sterile filtered so yeast or bacteria cannot spoil them.

causes.effect: malic acid becomes softer lactic acid
causes.result: lower perceived acidity, creamy and buttery notes

causes.effect: lees compounds dissolve into the wine

sections.heading: High-volume, inexpensive whites
points: Goal: easy-drinking, consistent, good value; not complex, not for ageing. Often blends labelled simply "dry white" or "fruity white".

Typical grapes: neutral and easy to ripen, such as Chardonnay and Pinot Grigio. Sauvignon Blanc is used too, rarely at the lowest prices; its vigour gives high yields, but herbaceous notes can dominate unripe fruit.
Grown in warm regions, so low acidity is common: acidification is one of the most frequent adjustments (flat, flabby Chardonnay otherwise).
Protective handling throughout; SO₂ monitored. Destem, crush, press.
Juice highly clarified, quickly (centrifuge or filter), to keep fruit.
Stainless steel, cool fermentation, commercial yeast for a fast, reliable ferment.
MLC usually blocked (chill + SO₂) and wine racked off the lees at once; a soft buttery Chardonnay may go through MLC.
Oak flavour from chips or staves in steel, not barrels (cost and time).
Often a little residual sugar (more often Chardonnay than Pinot Grigio): ferment dry, then add measured grape juice or RCGM.
Stabilised, fined and sterile filtered; SO₂ topped up at bottling.

sections.heading: Premium aromatic varieties
points: Sauvignon Blanc, Riesling, Muscat, Gewurztraminer, Torrontés. Aim: keep and show the primary fruit and floral aromas.
Crushed or whole bunch into the press, sometimes after a short skin contact. Juice cleaned gently (settling).
Inert vessels so nothing masks the fruit: stainless steel (New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling). Alsace Riesling may use large old oak (foudres): slight oxidation, more texture, no oak flavour.
Cool, slow fermentation. Sauvignon Blanc fermented dry.
Riesling from dry to luscious: stop the fermentation by chilling or SO₂ to keep sugar; with botrytised grapes it stops by itself.
No MLC (SO₂ straight after fermentation): keeps the high acidity and avoids buttery notes clashing with the fruit.
Bottled early; new oak avoided. Riesling may get lees contact, or up to a year in large old vats (Alsace, sometimes Germany).
Rarely blended. Exception: Sauvignon Blanc with Semillon for more body (Bordeaux, Western Australia).
Oaked Sauvignon Blanc (Pessac-Léognan, California Fumé Blanc): barrel fermentation, maybe ambient yeast, months on lees, MLC avoided, some new oak. Creamy and spicy.

causes.effect: nothing added on top of the fruit
causes.result: pure, pungent primary aromas and high acidity

causes.factor: Stopping fermentation by chilling or SO₂
causes.result: off-dry to sweet Riesling with low alcohol

sections.heading: Premium less-aromatic varieties
points: Chardonnay and Pinot Gris/Grigio are neutral, so the winemaker shapes the style: keep it pure, or build complexity and texture.
Whole-bunch pressing is common for Chardonnay. Some let the juice take in a little oxygen, thought to help ageing (it would strip an aromatic variety).
Gentle settling; some solids may be left for complexity and texture.

Vessels: stainless steel or concrete for fresh fruit (Chablis, north-east Italian Pinot Grigio, New Zealand Pinot Gris); large old oak (Alsace Pinot Gris); small new barrels for toast and roundness (Côte d’Or Chardonnay).
Pinot Gris with residual sugar: New Zealand stops the fermentation (chill or SO₂); in Alsace very ripe grapes may stop it naturally.

Oak after fermentation: new barriques give toast; older and larger barrels give gentle oxidation and complexity without much flavour. Some new oak is usual for Chardonnay (not Chablis); Pinot Gris mostly older oak.
MLC is used in almost all premium white Burgundy, Chablis included, to soften sharp acidity; avoided where fruit should lead.
Long fine-lees contact and lees stirring for a richer, rounder texture.
Usually not blended with other varieties.

causes.result: rounder, more complex wine that can age

topics.title: Red winemaking
topics.summary: Colour and tannin live in the skins, so reds ferment with them. Most choices are about how much colour, flavour and tannin to extract, and when.

sections.heading: How it differs from white
points: Black grapes ferment together with their skins to pick up colour, flavour and tannin.
So pressing comes after fermentation, not before, and there are many more choices before, during and after it.
Malolactic conversion is standard for reds; for whites it is a style choice.
Nearly all fruit is destemmed and crushed first. Whole bunches are the exception (see below).

causes.effect: colour, flavour and tannin dissolve into the wine

sections.heading: Before fermentation: cold soak
points: Crushed grapes can be held cool for a while before fermentation starts (cold maceration or cold soak).
It extracts colour and flavour. Tannin dissolves far better in alcohol, so little comes out at this stage.

causes.effect: colour and flavour extracted while there is no alcohol

sections.heading: Fermentation temperature
points: Reds ferment at about 20–32 °C, warmer than whites, to help extraction.
Above about 35 °C the yeast may die.
Temperature steers extraction. Cooling the vat near the end limits tannin pickup, even though rising alcohol makes tannin easier to extract.

causes.effect: more colour, flavour and tannin extracted

causes.factor: Cooling at the end of fermentation
causes.effect: less tannin extracted as alcohol rises

sections.heading: Cap management
points: Skins and pulp float up into a thick cap. Left floating, it gives up little, so it is worked back into the juice.
Extraction is set by the technique, how long it runs and how many times a day. Techniques are often combined or switched during fermentation.

Punching down: pushing the cap under, by hand with paddles or mechanically. Very extractive; too hard or too often, especially late on, gives bitter, astringent wine. By hand it carried a CO₂ risk for workers.
Pumping over: juice drawn from the bottom of the vat and pumped over the cap. Also cools the vat and adds oxygen.
Rack and return: all the juice drained into another vessel, then poured back over the cap. Very extractive, so usually only once or twice; good for cooling.
Rotary fermenters: horizontal tanks that turn, keeping skins and juice in constant contact.

causes.effect: tannin extracts most easily in alcohol

causes.factor: Pumping over or rack and return
causes.effect: juice moved and exposed to air

sections.heading: Fermentation vessels
points: Large vessels, often open-topped so the cap can be worked: oak, concrete or stainless steel.
Barrels are impractical for reds: the skins cannot be kept in contact with the juice.

sections.heading: After fermentation
points: Post-fermentation maceration keeps the wine on its skins for more tannin. How long depends on the style; very long macerations can make tannins smoother.
The free-run wine is drained off, then the skins are pressed: press wine.
Early press wine is close to free run; later fractions are darker and more tannic. They can be kept apart and blended back to adjust colour and tannin.

causes.result: firmer structure; very long ones can smooth tannins
used to build structure in the blend

sections.heading: Whole-bunch fermentation
points: Some or all of the fruit goes into the vat uncrushed. The stems must be ripe, or their tannins taste bitter.
Kept away from oxygen, whole berries make a little alcohol inside their cells without yeast (intracellular fermentation) and form distinctive fruity aromas.
Carbonic maceration: only whole bunches, vat filled with CO₂. At about 2% alcohol the skins split; the grapes are pressed and yeast finish the fermentation off the skins.
Carbonic taste: colour but little tannin. Soft and fruity, with kirsch, banana, bubblegum and cinnamon-like spice.

Semi-carbonic: whole bunches without added CO₂. Grapes at the bottom are crushed by the weight above, ambient yeast ferment that juice, and its CO₂ protects the intact berries, which go carbonic. Then pressed and finished off the skins.

Premium Pinot Noir variant: the whole bunches are punched down bit by bit over the first days and fermentation finishes on the skins. Carbonic notes blend better with the varietal fruit; fresher fruit.

Whole bunches with crushed fruit: the crushed grapes keep the bunches submerged, so they ferment inside the berries, and are broken up by punching down. More whole bunches means more carbonic character; silkier texture, brighter fruit.

causes.result: soft, fruity wine with kirsch, banana and bubblegum
bitter taste, so only ripe stems are used

sections.heading: Maturation, blending and clarification
points: The big maturation decision is oak or no oak: barrels, or staves and chips in an inert vessel.
Almost every red goes through MLC. Their stronger flavours gain less from long lees ageing than whites do.

Fewer producers now use only small new barrels; many mix barrel ages and larger sizes for subtler, better-integrated oak. Top wines still get more new oak, for longer, because their concentrated fruit can carry it.
Blending: grape varieties (colour, body, tannin, acidity, flavour), press wine into free run, wines from different oak (age, size, toast), or oaked with unoaked wine for a lighter oak touch.
Most reds are fined and/or filtered. Some producers skip it, believing it strips structure. Long maturation clears wine naturally as sediment settles.

causes.result: the best wines get more new oak for longer

sections.heading: High-volume, inexpensive reds
points: Grown in warm, sunny, dry regions. Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Syrah and Grenache suit them, and their skins give enough colour and fruit even at high yields.
Pinot Noir is rarely used: hard to grow, likes cool climates, and gives too little colour and tannin at high yields.
Next to premium versions: less colour, lighter tannin, simpler aromas. Varietal character fades, so wines can taste alike. Single variety or blend, sometimes labelled by style ("fruity red").
Target style: fruity, low tannin. Handled protectively with SO₂ checked throughout; destemmed and crushed; tartaric acid often added in hot regions. Cold soak only if vat space allows.

Commercial yeast at about 22–25 °C for fresh fruit; static or rotary vessels; cap worked lightly. No post-fermentation maceration (vat time, unwanted tannin). For more structure, macerate a small batch and blend it in.
Carbonic or semi-carbonic maceration also gives this style; common for inexpensive Grenache and basic Beaujolais.
Maturation: stainless steel for pure fruit, a few months in second- or third-fill barrels to soften tannin and add spice, or staves and chips in the tank for quick toasty notes.
Stabilised, fined and sterile filtered so they are bright with no sediment. SO₂ topped up at bottling, even though shelf life is short.

causes.factor: Lots of colour and flavour in the skins
causes.effect: still fruity and coloured at high yields
causes.result: Cabernet, Merlot, Syrah and Grenache suit volume wine

causes.factor: Thin-skinned Pinot Noir at high yields

sections.heading: Premium reds, grape by grape
points: Cabernet Sauvignon: destemmed (stems taste green), cold soak for colour, 26–30 °C, gentler extraction near the end, post-fermentation maceration to soften tannin. Lots of new French barriques, typically 12–18 months. Blended with Merlot (Shiraz in Australia).
Merlot: made like Cabernet, but its softer skins need less extraction. New oak suits its plum fruit; 12–18 months is common.

Pinot Noir: destemmed with a cold soak, or partly whole bunch. Ferments often go above 30 °C. Little post-fermentation maceration. 12–24 months in mostly used barrels; rarely blended with other grapes.

Syrah/Shiraz: powerful style from vigorous extraction of ripe grapes plus new oak; restrained style from earlier picking, gentle extraction, some whole bunches, long post-fermentation maceration and larger, older barrels.
Grenache: destemmed, cold soak, sometimes whole bunches; open-top steel or concrete; gentle punching down; usually drained at the end. Large old oak, since new oak swamps its fruit; usually blended.

topics.title: Rosé winemaking
topics.summary: Black grapes with only brief skin contact, or a dash of red in white. Three methods; oak is rarely used.

sections.heading: Direct pressing
points: Black grapes are crushed and pressed straight away, as for a white wine.
The skins give a little colour; care is needed not to extract tannin.
Gives the palest rosés.

sections.heading: Short maceration
points: Crushed black grapes sit on their skins until they have given the colour, flavour and tannin wanted. This can run into the start of fermentation.
The juice is then drained off the skins and fermented cool, like a white.

sections.heading: Blending
points: A little red wine is added to a white.
Not allowed in many European geographical indications; Champagne is the best-known exception.

topics.title: Sweet winemaking
topics.summary: Sweet wines keep unfermented sugar. Three routes: stop the fermentation, add something sweet, or concentrate the sugar in the grapes before fermentation.

sections.heading: Stopping the fermentation
points: Fortification: grape spirit kills the yeast; changes the wine’s whole balance (see fortified wines).
High dose of SO₂ or chilling, then filter out the yeast. Keep yeast away afterwards or fermentation restarts.
Used for premium German Kabinett and Spätlese, and sweet sparkling Asti.
Wines made this way are low in alcohol.

sections.heading: Adding a sweet component
points: Süssreserve: unfermented grape juice (kept from fermenting by filtering or SO₂) added to a dry wine before bottling. Common for medium-sweet German wines.
RCGM (rectified concentrated grape must) does the same job, often in high-volume inexpensive wines.

sections.heading: Concentrating the sugar in the grapes
points: All these methods concentrate acids and flavours along with the sugar.
Fermentation then stops by itself when the yeast cannot cope with so much sugar, sometimes as low as about 7% abv (German Trockenbeerenauslese).

sections.heading: Noble rot (Botrytis cinerea)
points: The same fungus as grey rot. Noble rot needs fully ripe grapes first, then humid misty mornings followed by dry, sunny afternoons.
The fungus pierces the skin; afternoon sun evaporates water, concentrating sugar, acid and flavour; the fungus adds its own flavours.
Taste: honey, apricot, citrus zest, dried fruit.
Spread is uneven, so several hand pickings (tries) are needed: costly, skilled work. Conditions do not come every year; too damp gives grey rot instead.
Examples: Sauternes, Tokaji, German and Austrian Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese. "Botrytised" on a label means noble rot.

causes.effect: noble rot develops but is held in check

causes.result: sweet wine with honey, apricot and zest, high acidity

sections.heading: Drying on the vine (passerillage)
points: After full ripeness, grapes left on the vine dehydrate towards raisins.
Needs a warm, dry autumn, otherwise grey rot.
Taste: over-ripe, dried and tropical fruit. Often labelled Late Harvest.

sections.heading: Drying after picking
points: Healthy picked grapes dry and lose water, concentrating sugar.
Needs warm, dry conditions; rotten grapes removed so rot cannot spread.
Italian passito wines such as Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG. Raisiny character.

sections.heading: Freezing on the vine
points: Healthy grapes hang into winter; at freezing, water in the pulp turns to ice.
Pressed frozen: the ice stays in the press, so the juice is sugar-rich.
Eiswein (Germany), Icewine (Canada). Very pure varietal character.
Can be imitated by freezing picked grapes in the winery.

topics.title: Sparkling winemaking
topics.summary: A second fermentation in a closed vessel traps CO₂. Where it happens (bottle or tank) and how long the wine stays on its lees decide the style: toasty and complex, or fresh and fruity.

sections.heading: Grapes and base wine
points: Grapes are picked early for high acidity, moderate sugar and delicate flavours; often hand-picked so whole bunches can be pressed gently.
Gentle pressing keeps colour and bitter phenolics out, especially from black grapes.
The base wine is dry, high in acidity, around 10–11% abv; it is often blended from many batches and vintages (reserve wines).

causes.factor: Early picking in a cool climate
causes.effect: high acidity, low sugar, neutral flavours
causes.result: base wine that balances the bubbles and suits autolysis

sections.heading: Traditional method
points: Liqueur de tirage (wine, sugar, yeast, nutrients) is added and the wine is bottled and capped. The second fermentation adds about 1.5% abv and around 6 atmospheres of pressure.
The wine then ages on its lees in bottle. Yeast autolysis slowly gives bread, biscuit, brioche and toast, and finer bubbles.
Riddling (by hand on pupitres or by gyropalette) moves the lees into the neck; disgorgement freezes the neck and the pressure pushes the plug out.
Dosage (wine and sugar) sets the final sweetness, then the cork and wire go on.
Used for Champagne, Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta and most premium New World and English sparkling wine.

causes.factor: Long ageing on the lees in bottle
causes.result: biscuit, brioche and toast; creamier mousse

sections.heading: Transfer method
points: Second fermentation and lees ageing in bottle as above, but the wine is then emptied into a pressurised tank, filtered, dosed and rebottled.
Keeps some autolytic character without riddling; used for unusual bottle sizes and some New World wines.

sections.heading: Tank method
points: The second fermentation happens in a sealed pressure tank, then the wine is filtered, dosed and bottled under pressure.
Fast and cheap, with little or no lees contact, so primary fruit and floral aromas stay in front.
Used for Prosecco, most Sekt and many inexpensive sparkling wines.

causes.factor: Second fermentation in tank, short lees contact

sections.heading: Asti method and carbonation
points: Asti method: a single fermentation of Muscat juice in a sealed tank; CO₂ is kept and the fermentation is stopped by chilling at about 7–9.5% abv.
Result: sweet, low alcohol, intensely grapey (Asti spumante; Moscato d’Asti is lightly sparkling at about 5%).
Carbonation: CO₂ injected like a soft drink; large bubbles that fade quickly; only for the cheapest wines.

sections.heading: Sweetness terms (EU)
points: Brut Nature 0–3 g/L; Extra Brut 0–6; Brut 0–12; Extra Dry 12–17; Sec 17–32; Demi-Sec 32–50; Doux over 50.
Extra Dry is sweeter than Brut: a common exam trap.

topics.title: Sparkling wines of the world
topics.summary: Champagne sets the benchmark; Crémant, Cava, Franciacorta, England and the New World use the same method, while Prosecco, Asti and Sekt show the fresher tank-method styles.

sections.heading: Champagne
points: Cold northern climate and chalk soils give high-acid, low-sugar grapes: Chardonnay (finesse), Pinot Noir (body, structure) and Meunier (fruit).
Pressing is strictly limited: 4,000 kg of grapes give at most 2,550 L, split into the cuvée (first, finest juice) and the taille.
Non-vintage: at least 15 months from bottling to release, 12 of them on lees; vintage: at least 3 years. Many houses age far longer.
Non-vintage blends many villages and reserve wines to keep a house style; vintage wines show one year; prestige cuvées are the top blends.
Styles: Blanc de Blancs (Chardonnay only), Blanc de Noirs (black grapes only), rosé (usually by blending red wine into white), sweetness from Brut Nature to Doux.
Label codes: NM (négociant-manipulant, the houses), RM (récoltant-manipulant, growers), CM (co-operative).

causes.effect: drainage, water reserve, cool steady ageing

sections.heading: Crémant
points: Traditional-method French sparkling from outside Champagne: Alsace (Pinot Blanc), Loire (Chenin), Burgundy (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir), Limoux and others.
At least 9 months on lees; whole-bunch pressing; usually fresher and fruitier, less autolytic, and cheaper than Champagne.

sections.heading: Cava
points: Traditional method, mostly from Penedès; Macabeo (fruit), Xarel·lo (body) and Parellada (freshness), plus Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.
Warmer climate: riper fruit, lower acidity, a little earthy; at least 9 months on lees, Reserva 18, Gran Reserva 30.

sections.heading: Prosecco, Asti and Sekt
points: Prosecco: tank method from Glera in Veneto and Friuli; fresh pear, apple and blossom; Brut or Extra Dry. Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOCG hills give finer wines.
Asti and Moscato d’Asti: Muscat, Asti method, sweet and low in alcohol.
Sekt: Germany’s sparkling, mostly tank method; Deutscher Sekt must use German grapes; the best are traditional-method Riesling or Pinot.

sections.heading: Franciacorta, England and the New World
points: Franciacorta: traditional method in Lombardy; riper and rounder than Champagne; Satèn is a softer, lower-pressure style.
England: chalk soils and a cool climate close to Champagne’s; high-acid traditional-method wines from the three Champagne grapes.
New World: cool sites chosen for acidity: Tasmania, Adelaide Hills, Yarra (Australia); Marlborough (NZ); Carneros, Anderson Valley (California); Cap Classique (South Africa).
Warmer New World climates give riper fruit and less acidity, so many producers rely more on fruit than long autolysis.

topics.title: Sherry
topics.summary: A dry, neutral Palomino base wine is fortified and aged in a solera, either under flor (biological ageing) or exposed to oxygen (oxidative ageing). Sweet styles come from PX, Moscatel or sweetening.

sections.heading: Vineyard and base wine
points: The Jerez triangle: Jerez de la Frontera, Sanlúcar de Barrameda and El Puerto de Santa María. Hot summers; humid Atlantic poniente wind near the coast.
Albariza: white, chalky soil that soaks up winter rain and keeps it through the summer.
Palomino gives a neutral, low-acid base wine fermented to dryness at about 11–12.5% abv. Free-run juice goes to Fino; heavier press juice to Oloroso.

sections.heading: Classification and fortification
points: Each cask of new wine is tasted and classified: the most delicate for biological ageing, fuller ones for oxidative ageing.
Biological: fortified to about 15–15.5% so flor yeast can survive. Oxidative: fortified to about 17%, which kills flor.

sections.heading: Flor and biological ageing
points: Flor is a layer of yeast on the wine’s surface in part-filled casks. It needs alcohol below about 15.5%, humidity and moderate temperatures.
It shields the wine from oxygen and consumes glycerol, alcohol and nutrients, giving a pale, light-bodied, bone-dry wine with bready, almond notes and acetaldehyde.
Fino (Jerez, El Puerto) and Manzanilla (Sanlúcar, where the sea humidity keeps flor thick all year, giving an even lighter, saltier style).
Drink fresh and chilled once opened.

causes.result: pale, light, dry, bready and almond (Fino, Manzanilla)

sections.heading: The solera
points: Rows of casks of different ages: wine for bottling is drawn from the oldest level (the solera) and topped up from the next (criaderas), down to the youngest.
Fractional blending keeps the style consistent and feeds flor with fresh nutrients. Minimum average age is two years.

sections.heading: Styles
points: Amontillado: starts as Fino; when flor dies (or the wine is refortified to about 17%) it ages oxidatively. Amber, dry, with both bready and nutty notes.
Oloroso: oxidative only. Deep brown, full-bodied, dry, walnut, toffee, leather; alcohol rises as water evaporates.
Palo Cortado: rare; the delicacy of Amontillado with the body of Oloroso.
Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel: sun-dried grapes, fortified, aged oxidatively: very sweet, raisin, fig, coffee.
Sweetened blends: Pale Cream (Fino + sugar), Medium (Amontillado-based), Cream (Oloroso + PX).
Age-dated: VOS (20+ years) and VORS (30+ years); also 12 and 15 years.

topics.title: Port
topics.summary: Black grapes from the hot Douro valley are fermented briefly with intense extraction, then fortified to stop fermentation. Ruby styles keep fruit; tawny styles age oxidatively in small casks.

sections.heading: The Douro
points: Hot, dry, continental valley sheltered from the Atlantic by mountains; gets hotter and drier further east (Baixo Corgo, Cima Corgo, Douro Superior).
Schist soils on steep terraces; schist splits vertically so roots reach water.
Main grapes: Touriga Nacional, Touriga Franca, Tinta Roriz (Tempranillo), Tinta Barroca, Tinto Cão — thick-skinned and rich in colour and tannin.

sections.heading: Making Port
points: Fermentation lasts only two or three days, so extraction must be fast and intense: foot treading in stone lagares, robotic lagares or autovinifiers.
At about 6–9% abv the wine is drained onto grape spirit (about 77% abv), roughly 1 part spirit to 4 parts wine, giving 19–22% abv and plenty of sugar.
Traditionally aged in Vila Nova de Gaia, cooler and more humid than the Douro.

causes.factor: Fortification after two or three days

causes.result: treading and lagares to get colour and tannin quickly

sections.heading: Ruby styles (fruit kept)
points: Aged in large vats with little oxygen: deep colour and black-fruit flavours.
Ruby: young, simple, fruity. Reserve: better quality, aged a little longer.
Late Bottled Vintage (LBV): one year, bottled 4–6 years after harvest; usually filtered and ready to drink.
Vintage Port: only in declared years, bottled after about 2 years, unfiltered; needs decades in bottle and decanting. Single Quinta Vintage: one estate, often in undeclared years.
Crusted: a blend of years, bottled unfiltered, throws a sediment.

causes.factor: Bottle ageing of unfiltered Vintage Port
causes.result: fruit with dried fruit, spice and a heavy sediment

sections.heading: Tawny styles (oxidative)
points: Aged in small casks (pipes, about 550 L) for years: colour fades to amber, flavours turn to nuts, caramel and dried fruit.
Basic Tawny is a lighter, cheaper blend; age-indicated Tawnies are 10, 20, 30 or 40 Year Old (an average style, not a minimum).
Colheita: tawny from one year, at least 7 years in wood.
White Port (often served with tonic) and Rosé Port are also made.

causes.result: amber colour, walnut, toffee and dried fruit; ready to drink when bottled

topics.title: Madeira and vins doux naturels
topics.summary: Madeira is deliberately heated and oxidised, so it barely changes once opened. Vins doux naturels are French wines fortified early in fermentation to keep their sweetness.

sections.heading: Madeira: vineyards and grapes
points: Subtropical Atlantic island: humid, with fungal disease pressure; steep terraces (poios) worked by hand.
Named grapes set the sweetness: Sercial (dry), Verdelho (medium-dry), Bual or Boal (medium-sweet), Malmsey or Malvasia (sweet). All keep very high acidity.
Tinta Negra is the most planted grape and is used for most blends.

sections.heading: Madeira: making and ageing
points: Fortified with grape spirit (to about 17–22%): early for sweet styles, late for dry ones.
Estufagem: tanks heated to about 45–50 °C for at least three months; quick, for younger wines.
Canteiro: casks left in warm lofts for years; slower, finer, for the best wines.
Styles: blends sold by age (5, 10, 15, 20 years and more), Colheita (one year, at least 5 years in cask), Frasqueira (vintage, at least 20 years in cask).

causes.result: brown, tangy, caramel and nutty; lasts for months once opened

sections.heading: Vins doux naturels
points: Grape spirit is added early in fermentation, keeping lots of sugar; about 15–18% abv.
Muscat VDN (Beaumes-de-Venise, Rivesaltes, Frontignan): kept away from oxygen and bottled young: fresh grape, orange blossom, peach.
Grenache VDN (Banyuls, Maury, Rivesaltes): unoxidised (Rimage, Grenat: red fruit) or oxidatively aged, sometimes outdoors in glass bonbonnes (Tuilé, Ambré, Hors d’Âge: dried fruit, nuts, rancio).
Rutherglen Muscat (Australia) is a related fortified style: very ripe, raisined grapes, years of hot oxidative ageing; graded Rutherglen, Classic, Grand, Rare.

topics.title: Wine law and labels
topics.summary: Geographical indications tell you where a wine is from and which rules it follows. The EU has two levels (PDO and PGI); each country adds its own terms.

sections.heading: EU categories
points: PDO (Protected Designation of Origin): smaller areas, stricter rules on grapes, yields, methods and ageing.
PGI (Protected Geographical Indication): larger areas, more freedom (varieties, yields).
Wine without a GI can show variety and vintage (e.g. Vin de France).
If a vintage, variety or region is on the label, at least 85% of the wine must match.

sections.heading: Country terms
points: France: AOC / AOP (PDO), IGP (PGI, e.g. Pays d’Oc), Vin de France. Burgundy adds Premier Cru and Grand Cru; Bordeaux uses classifications such as the 1855 Médoc Crus Classés.
Italy: DOCG and DOC (PDO), IGT (PGI). Classico = the historic heart; Superiore = higher alcohol or stricter rules; Riserva = longer ageing.
Spain: DOCa (Rioja, Priorat), DO, Vino de Pago (single estate) for PDO; Vino de la Tierra for PGI.
Germany: Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein (PDO), Landwein (PGI). Prädikat levels by grape sugar at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Trockenbeerenauslese, Eiswein.
Austria: DAC for regional typicity; Portugal: DOC and Vinho Regional; Hungary: OEM.

sections.heading: Ageing terms in Spain
points: Joven: little or no oak. Roble: some oak, not regulated as strictly.
Red Crianza: at least 2 years of ageing, 6 months in oak (Rioja and Ribera del Duero: 1 year in oak).
Red Reserva: at least 3 years, 1 in oak. Red Gran Reserva: at least 5 years, 18 months in oak (Rioja: 2 years in oak).

sections.heading: Outside Europe
points: Most New World countries define geographical boundaries but few rules on grapes or yields.
USA: AVAs; a variety on the label needs at least 75% of it; an AVA needs 85%; a vintage with an AVA needs 95%.
Australia: GIs (zones, regions, sub-regions) and an 85% rule for variety, vintage and GI.
South Africa: Wine of Origin (regions, districts, wards); New Zealand and Chile: GIs and DOs, with 85% rules.

sections.heading: Other label terms
points: Sweetness words: sec / trocken / seco (dry), demi-sec / halbtrocken / feinherb (off-dry to medium), moelleux, doux, dolce (sweet).
"Old vines", "Reserve" and "Estate" have no legal meaning in most countries.
Organic and biodynamic claims need certification.

topics.title: France: wine law and classifications
topics.summary: Three national categories, then each region’s own ladder. Bordeaux ranks estates (châteaux), Burgundy ranks vineyards, and Alsace, Beaujolais and the Rhône have simple tiers of their own.

sections.heading: National categories
points: PDO: Appellation d’origine protégée (AOP), usually still written Appellation d’origine contrôlée (AC / AOC) on labels.
PGI: Indication géographique protégée (IGP); the old term Vin de Pays (VdP) is still seen.
No GI: Vin de France.
One plot can belong to a generic and a more prestigious appellation. Producers register each year which one they will use, so a weak vintage can be sold under the lesser name.

sections.heading: Bordeaux: the appellations
points: Over 50 appellations, from generic Bordeaux to small communes. They do not form a quality ladder like Burgundy’s, so group them by style.
Generic: Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur (stricter rules, higher minimum alcohol) for reds; Bordeaux for whites; Bordeaux Rosé and Clairet (longer maceration, deeper, fuller).
Left Bank (west and south of the Gironde and Garonne): Médoc, Haut-Médoc and its communes, Graves, Pessac-Léognan, Sauternes.
Between the rivers: Entre-Deux-Mers (white only). Right Bank: Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and their satellites, and the Côtes de Bordeaux group.
Top Médoc estates make dry whites that can only be sold as Bordeaux.

causes.factor: Leading châteaux make second and third wines
causes.effect: weaker vats are kept out of the grand vin
causes.result: consistent top wine; surplus may go to négociants

sections.heading: Bordeaux: the classifications
points: They rank estates, not vineyards, and (except in Saint-Émilion) sit outside the appellation system. An estate can buy or sell land, so a château name is more a brand than a plot.

1855 Classification (made for the Paris Exhibition): Médoc reds in five ranks; first growths Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Mouton Rothschild, plus Haut-Brion from Graves. Sauternes in three ranks, with Yquem alone at the top.
Almost unchanged since 1855, so how well it reflects quality today is debated. Classified estates are crus classés.
Cru Bourgeois (Médoc): three tiers, Cru Bourgeois, Supérieur and Exceptionnel; reviewed every five years.
Graves: separate red and white lists with no ranking: all are simply crus classés. All now lie in Pessac-Léognan, created after the list was drawn up.

Saint-Émilion: built into the appellations. Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation; within it, Grand Cru Classé, then Premier Grand Cru Classé B and A. Reviewed about every ten years, with promotion and demotion.

causes.effect: the land behind a name can change
causes.result: reputation follows the château, not the plot

sections.heading: Burgundy: the hierarchy
points: Regional (about half of production): Bourgogne Rouge and Blanc from anywhere; narrower regional names such as Bourgogne Hautes Côtes de Nuits / de Beaune, Bourgogne Côte d’Or, Bourgogne Côte Chalonnaise; Mâcon and Mâcon-Villages.
Some regional wine is declassified from better appellations because of high yields or a producer’s choice.
Commune or village (about a third): e.g. Chablis, Gevrey-Chambertin. A non-classified single vineyard may be named after the village.
Premier cru (over 600 vineyards, about a tenth): label says Premier Cru plus the vineyard, or no vineyard if several are blended from one village.
Grand cru (33: 32 in the Côte d’Or, one in Chablis split into seven climats; just over 1%): only the vineyard name appears, with Grand Cru.
Most vineyards have several owners; one with a single owner is a monopole.
Gamay may be used in some regional wines; reds at village level and above must be Pinot Noir.

causes.effect: better drainage, sun and less frost
causes.result: they hold the premier and grand cru vineyards

sections.heading: Beaujolais and the Rhône
points: Beaujolais: Beaujolais (southern plain), Beaujolais-Villages (39 villages on the northern granite hills, usually blended, village names rarely shown), then ten crus, each its own appellation.
Beaujolais Nouveau: Beaujolais or Beaujolais-Villages only; released on the third Thursday of November, not sold by producers after 31 August of the next year. Crus may not be sold as Nouveau.

Rhône: Côtes du Rhône (over half of the south’s appellation wine), Côtes du Rhône Villages (lower yields, higher minimum alcohol, more Grenache, Syrah and Mourvèdre), Villages plus a village name (100% from that village; e.g. Séguret), then the crus.
Named villages can apply to become crus, as Gigondas and Vacqueyras did.

sections.heading: Alsace and the Loire
points: Alsace: two appellations for still wine, Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru. A named grape means 100% of it.

Alsace Grand Cru: over 50 vineyards, usually one noble grape (Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Gris, Muscat); vineyard, vintage and grape on the label. Some boundaries are thought too wide, so some top producers ignore the term.
Vendanges Tardives (late harvest, dry to medium-sweet) and Sélection de Grains Nobles (higher sugar, usually noble rot, sweet): noble grapes only, minimum ripeness by variety.
Since the 2021 harvest the back label must state sweetness: sec, demi-sec, moelleux or doux. Terms like Réserve personnelle have no legal meaning. Blends are Edelzwicker or Gentil.
Loire: no region-wide appellation; IGP Val de Loire covers it. Four sub-regions (Nantais, Anjou-Saumur, Touraine, Central Vineyards) are not appellations.

topics.title: Italy: labels, ageing rules and passito
topics.summary: Italy uses DOC and DOCG for PDO wine and IGT for PGI. Classico marks the original zone, Riserva longer ageing; the big reds have minimum ageing before release, and the Veneto concentrates wines by drying grapes.

sections.heading: Categories
points: PDO is DOP in Italian, but labels mostly show the traditional terms: DOC (set area, grapes and methods) and DOCG (all DOC rules plus stricter ones, and in most cases bottled in the area).
PGI is IGP, but the older term IGT is more common, e.g. Toscana IGT, Veneto IGT, Puglia IGT, Terre Siciliane IGT.
Super Tuscans showed that great wine could sit outside the PDO rules; many are still Toscana IGT, though Bolgheri and Maremma Toscana DOC now allow all-international blends.

sections.heading: Classico and Riserva
points: Classico: many appellations grew beyond their historic area. Classico wines come only from the original zone and include many of the best (Soave Classico, Valpolicella Classico, Chianti Classico).
Chianti Classico is its own DOCG, not a sub-zone of Chianti DOCG. Chianti’s seven sub-zones (e.g. Rufina, Colli Senesi) may add their name to the label.
Riserva: higher minimum alcohol and longer ageing than the basic wine.

sections.heading: Ageing rules to know
points: Barolo DOCG: 100% Nebbiolo; at least 38 months, 18 in wood; released from 1 January of the fourth year after harvest.
Barbaresco DOCG: at least 26 months, 9 in wood; released from 1 January of the third year.
Brunello di Montalcino DOCG: 100% Sangiovese; at least 2 years in wood; released from 1 January of the fifth year. Declassified: Rosso di Montalcino DOC.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG: Sangiovese plus permitted grapes; at least 2 years’ ageing. Declassified: Rosso di Montepulciano DOC.
Chianti Classico: 12 months before release; Riserva 24 months (3 in bottle); Gran Selezione: single estate, 6 months more than Riserva. No oak rule, though most see oak.

causes.factor: Long minimum ageing for high-tannin grapes
causes.result: wines closer to drinkable, with tertiary notes starting

sections.heading: Village and vineyard names in Piemonte
points: Barolo is often a blend of villages; a single village can be named, e.g. Barolo Serralunga d’Alba.
The best wines come from named vineyards (crus), e.g. Barolo Cannubi. Barbaresco works the same way.
Other grapes from these hills (Dolcetto, Barbera) go out as Alba DOC or Langhe DOC.
Many Piemonte names are grape plus town: Barbera d’Asti DOCG, Barbera d’Alba DOC, Dolcetto d’Alba DOC.

sections.heading: Passito and ripasso (Veneto)
points: Passito: grapes picked early (high acid), dried indoors to concentrate sugar and flavour, fermented in winter. Adds structure, flavour and, for reds, colour.
Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG: fermented dry or off-dry; full body, high alcohol, medium to high tannin, intense red berry and spice; usually aged in large casks.
Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG: so sweet that fermentation stops on its own; sweet, full, red or white.

Ripasso: Amarone is drained off its skins just before fermentation ends; finished Valpolicella goes onto those unpressed skins, and their leftover sugar ferments, adding colour, flavour and tannin. Valpolicella Ripasso DOC: medium to full, stewed cherry and plum.

causes.effect: water evaporates, sugar and flavour concentrate
extra extraction and a little more alcohol
causes.result: Ripasso sits between Valpolicella and Amarone

sections.heading: Vineyards: pergola and bush vines
points: North: high-yielding vines at low density on pergolas: canopy overhead, grapes hanging below in shade with good airflow, so less sunburn and rot.
Pergolas are kept where high acid and low sugar are wanted (sparkling base) and for grapes to be dried, which must be healthy; elsewhere denser VSP plantings now dominate.
South: traditionally low bush vines shaded by their own leaves; old vines remain, but cordon training on trellises is now usual and allows machines on Puglia’s plain.

topics.title: Spain and Portugal: labels, ageing and regions
topics.summary: Spain layers DO, DOCa and Vino de Pago over PGI Vino de la Tierra, and defines ageing terms from Joven to Gran Reserva. Portugal uses DOC and Vinho Regional; learn its five main DOCs and the big Vinho Regional areas.

sections.heading: Spain: categories
points: PDO is DOP, but labels mostly show the traditional terms.
DO: rules on grapes, viticulture and area.
DOCa: a DO of at least 10 years’ standing can apply for promotion. Only two: Rioja and Priorat (DOQ, the Catalan form).
Vino de Pago (VP): a few single estates with high reputations; only their own grapes, made and aged on the estate. Most are in La Mancha.
PGI: Vino de la Tierra (VdlT); Castilla y León is the largest. No GI: Vino.

sections.heading: Spain: ageing terms
points: Joven: no minimum ageing; in Rioja the term is Genérico.
Crianza: red 24 months total, 6 in barrel; white and rosé 18 months total.
Reserva: red 36 months, 12 in barrel; white and rosé 24 months, 6 in barrel.
Gran Reserva: red 60 months, 18 in barrel; white and rosé 48 months, 6 in barrel. Only in exceptional vintages; whites and rosés rarely.
These are national minimums; some regions (such as Rioja) ask for more, and many producers exceed them.

causes.result: vanilla and coconut (American oak) or spice (French) leading to leather and dried fruit

sections.heading: Spain: six groups of regions
points: Upper Ebro: Rioja, Navarra, Cariñena, Calatayud.
Catalunya: Penedès, Priorat; DO Catalunya covers the whole region; nearly all Cava.
Duero Valley: Ribera del Duero, Toro, Rueda.
North West: Rías Baixas, Bierzo.
Levante: Valencia, Jumilla, Yecla.
Castilla-La Mancha: La Mancha, Valdepeñas.

sections.heading: Spain: the climate challenge
points: North and north-west: moderate, maritime, wet. East coast: warm Mediterranean, hotter further south. Meseta Central: hot continental, freezing winters, little rain.
Everywhere but the north-west, heat and drought matter most; fungal disease is rare.
Low-density bush vines give each vine more water and shade the grapes; wires are slowly being added for machine harvesting.
High altitude (Ribera del Duero over 850 m) gives cool nights that keep acidity.

causes.factor: Water stress on a hot plateau
causes.effect: vines planted far apart and bush-trained
causes.result: low yields per hectare even where vineyards are vast

sections.heading: Portugal: categories and regions
points: PDO: DOP, but DOC is widely used. PGI: IGP, often shown as Vinho Regional. No GI: Vinho, which includes much simple, fruity off-dry rosé.
The five main DOCs: Vinho Verde, Douro, Dão, Bairrada, Alentejo.
Big Vinho Regional areas: Lisboa (largest by volume), Alentejano (wider than Alentejo DOC), Península de Setúbal and Tejo. Looser rules, more grapes, including international ones.
The same grape may change name between regions: Tempranillo is Tinta Roriz in the north and Aragonês in the Alentejo; Mencía is Jaen in Dão; Albariño is Alvarinho.

sections.heading: Vinho Verde alcohol rules
points: Classic white Vinho Verde: 8–11.5% abv, high acid, often a slight spritz; the lowest-alcohol wines are usually off-dry.
With a grape, sub-region or quality term on the label: up to 14% abv.
Vinho Verde Alvarinho: 100% Alvarinho from Monção e Melgaço, 11.5–14% abv, riper and more tropical.

topics.title: Germany, Austria, Tokaj, Greece: labels and styles
topics.summary: Germany and Austria grade wine by grape sugar at harvest (Prädikat) and by origin; Austria adds DACs for regional typicity. Tokaj defines its sweet styles by residual sugar; Greece follows the EU PDO/PGI model.

sections.heading: Germany: categories
points: Deutscher Wein (no GI), Landwein (PGI), Qualitätswein (PDO). Almost all German wine is PDO.
Qualitätswein must come from one of 13 winegrowing areas (Anbaugebiete), named on the label. Dry wines of every colour and quality level are often just Qualitätswein.
Prädikatswein is a step within Qualitätswein: higher minimum must weight, six levels. In rising order: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Trockenbeerenauslese.
Kabinett and Spätlese: dry to medium-sweet; Auslese: dry to sweet; BA, Eiswein, TBA: sweet only. Think of the levels as styles.

causes.effect: pickers pass through the vineyard several times
causes.result: several Prädikat levels from one site in one year

sections.heading: Germany: sweetness and origin on the label
points: trocken = dry; halbtrocken = off-dry to medium; feinherb is used instead by some but has no legal definition. Often sweetness has to be guessed from the category or the alcohol.
Since 2021 (five-year transition): winegrowing area → Region (the word Region on the label) → village → single vineyard, e.g. Piesport (village) vs Piesporter Goldtröpfchen (vineyard).
Before this, some wide areas could be named like single vineyards, which confused buyers.
Single vineyards can also be Erstes Gewächs or Grosses Gewächs: always dry, stricter rules (strictest for Grosses Gewächs).

sections.heading: Germany: the VDP
points: A growers’ association with its own vineyard classification covering most of Germany’s best sites and strict rules; an eagle on the capsule.
VDP.Erste Lage and VDP.Grosse Lage (best sites); a dry wine from a Grosse Lage is VDP.Grosses Gewächs, marked GG with a grape bunch on the bottle neck.
VDP.Grosses Gewächs is a VDP trademark, not part of German law, but these are seen as Germany’s best dry wines. Permitted grapes vary by region.

sections.heading: Austria
points: Wein (no GI), Landwein (PGI), Qualitätswein (PDO): almost all Austrian wine is PDO.
Qualitätswein from a generic region (Niederösterreich, Burgenland, Steiermark, Wien) or a specified region: 40 permitted grapes, any style.

DAC (Districtus Austriae Controllatus, since 2002): growers agree on grapes and styles that typify their area; only wines in that style may use the DAC name. Others are labelled with the generic region. Village or single-vineyard names may appear within a DAC.

Most specified regions are now DACs, e.g. Weinviertel (Grüner Veltliner, Klassik or Reserve), Wachau, Kamptal, Kremstal, Neusiedlersee (Zweigelt), Leithaberg and Mittelburgenland (Blaufränkisch), Ruster Ausbruch (sweet, TBA level).
Prädikat levels work as in Germany but are mostly for medium-sweet and sweet wines; Austria adds Strohwein / Schilfwein (grapes dried on straw or reeds over winter).

causes.factor: DAC rules tie a name to a style

sections.heading: Tokaj: styles and rules
points: Dry wines (usually Furmint), 75 cl bottles; sweet wines traditionally in 50 cl bottles.

Szamorodni ("as it comes"): partly botrytised bunches, dry (száraz) or sweet (édes); at least six months in cask, released from January of the second year. Dry ones age under a flor-like yeast in part-filled casks: Fino-like.
Tokaji Aszú: aszú berries macerated 12–60 hours in base wine or must (whole berries avoid bitterness), pressed, then at least 18 months in oak. More berries, more sweetness.
Since 2013: 5 puttonyos = at least 120 g/L sugar (the minimum for Aszú), 6 puttonyos = at least 150 g/L; 3 or 4 puttonyos may still appear but must also reach 120 g/L.
Eszencia: only the free-run juice of aszú berries, at least 450 g/L sugar; ferments for years to under about 5% abv; lives a century.
Modern Late Harvest: grapes left long on the vine, botrytised or not, fermented like Sauternes rather than macerated; shorter ageing.

sections.heading: Greece
points: EU system: PDO and PGI. Dry PDO wines may say Protected Designation of Origin or, less often, Appellation d’origine de qualité supérieure; at home, Prostatevomeni Onomasia Proelefsis.
Three PDOs lead exports, each tied to one grape: Naoussa (Xinomavro), Nemea (Agiorgitiko), Santorini (Assyrtiko).

topics.title: Storage, service and food
topics.summary: Keep wine cool, dark and still; serve it at the right temperature; spot faults; and match the food’s sweetness, acidity, salt, umami and heat to the wine.

sections.heading: Storage
points: Cool and constant (about 10–15 °C), dark, away from vibration and strong smells; bottles with corks lie flat so the cork stays moist.
Heat speeds ageing and can push corks out; light can cause "light strike" in clear bottles.

sections.heading: Serving temperatures
points: Sweet wines and sparkling: well chilled, about 6–10 °C.
Light, aromatic and simple whites: 7–10 °C. Medium to full and oaked whites: 10–13 °C.
Light reds (Beaujolais): about 13 °C, lightly chilled. Medium to full reds: 15–18 °C.
Too cold hides aromas and makes tannins harsher; too warm makes alcohol stand out.

sections.heading: Opening, decanting and faults
points: Decant to remove sediment (Vintage Port, old reds) or to let young wines breathe.
Open sparkling wine by holding the cork and turning the bottle, at an angle, with no pop.

Faults: cork taint (TCA, musty wet cardboard), oxidation (brown, flat, nutty in a wine that should be fresh), reduction (rotten egg, cabbage), Brettanomyces (farmyard, plasters), volatile acidity (vinegar, nail polish).
Keep opened wine with less air: stopper and fridge, inert gas or vacuum. Fortified wines like Madeira and Tawny last longest.

sections.heading: Food and wine
points: Sweetness in food makes wine taste drier, more acidic and more bitter: the wine should be at least as sweet.
Umami (mushrooms, aged cheese, cured meat) makes wine taste more bitter, acidic and alcoholic and less fruity.
Acidity and salt in food make wine taste softer, fuller and fruitier: high-acid wines suit acidic or salty dishes.
Chilli heat increases the burn of alcohol and bitterness of tannin: choose low alcohol, low tannin, some sweetness.
Fat and oil are cut by acidity and softened by tannin; bitterness adds to bitterness.
Match intensity: delicate food with delicate wine, powerful with powerful.
